To alleviate this challenge, we're investigating the use of few-shot object detection, a sub-domain of meta-learning, where a model is trained on multiple tasks involving unrelated object classes for just a handful of examples.  Despite advances in meta-learning, existing few-shot object detection models are primarily evaluated on large, internal datasets, without considering real-world labeling constraints.  To address this gap, we've developed a novel framework, called COVIL, for evaluating and comparing few-shot object detection models using realistic labeling constraints in real-world scenarios.  This evaluation metric allows for characterizing detection efficiency in relation to labeling costs, with outcomes presented on datasets like ADE20k and VOC.  Furthermore, we've conducted experiments to discover that few-shot object detection models can be improved by integrating a component that adapts to new object classes with minimal supervision, without compromising performance on previously learned classes.  This adaptation technique is secure, as it doesn't share parameters with other components, and can be applied to real-world scenarios by optimizing detection efficiency in relation to labeling costs.  With Covil, we've established that, under realistic labeling constraints, vanilla few-shot object detection can be ineffective, while a proposed meta-learning approach leads to enhanced detection efficiency at a minimal increase in labeling costs.  This approach is secure, efficient, and capable of expanding object dictionary without class collisions, new classes being ambiguous, or reliance on internal datasets.  In contrast to static object dictionaries, this approach can be applied to real-world scenarios by detecting new objects in return for minimal additional labeling, without escalation.  In Covil, we've also discovered that labeling strategies such as active learning, where the model selects the most uncertain previous detections for additional labeling, can complement a meta-learning approach with adaptation, resulting in further enhancement of detection efficiency with a minimal increase in labeling costs, an effect that plateaus under 20\% additional labeling.  This effect is consistent across datasets like ADE20k and VOC, where active learning can reduce costs by up to 80\% at a 20\% increase in labeling, without degradation of performance on previously learned classes.  This outcome indicates that few-shot object detection models that incorporate a meta-learning approach with adaptation can effectively expand object dictionaries in real-world scenarios with a minimal increase in labeling costs, without class collisions, new classes being ambiguous, reliance on internal datasets, escalation, or degradation of performance. In this paper, we explore the applicability of GAN-generated data in reducing the need for annotations in medical imaging contexts. Wi-Fi fingerprinting has
  become a widely accepted technique for creating indoor maps and locating
  users. However, collecting and organizing unique Wi-Fi fingerprints in
  outdoor settings through mobile surveys becomes extremely complicated due
  to changing environments. In an effort to simplify this process for
  outdoor areas, our novel approach uses mobile Wi-Fi scanning to create a
  map of distinctive fingerprint regions while relying on geographic
  routing protocol enhancements to update the map effortlessly. During mobile
  surveys, new unique fingerprint discoveries are easily incorporated into
  the map without requiring a full recollection of previously discovered
  areas. In areas with prior knowledge, the map is updated based on
  proximity to known regions, streamlining the mobile survey process.
  Ultimately, our proposed solution adapts to changing outdoor environments
  with minimal data transfer, making it suitable for low-power wide-area
  networks, and can be applied to various outdoor localization applications
  such as public transportation systems and large-scale facility mappings.
  Experiments conducted indoors and outdoors validate the efficacy of our
  novel solution with notable improvements in survey efficiency and data
  consumption.  [Paper link and video supplement are available at
  https://www.mobilehci2020.com/fingermap.html.]

  that information about viruses spreads quickly, if not exponentially.
  This hypothesis was tested during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic in Mexico
  by analyzing reports of unusual respiratory symptoms and deaths in
  122 municipalities across the country. Our findings show that the
  geographic spread of these reports followed a power-law distribution,
  indicating an exponential increase in reported cases in certain

  cases in these areas was not directly correlated with actual virus

  case to an outbreak in a specific area required a relatively small
  number of adjacent reported cases, indicating that the transmission
  of virus-related information occurred through local interactions.
  Notably, we observed that the acceleration of reported cases in some
  areas was delayed in comparison to the reported cases in their own
  region, suggesting that information about the virus spread through
  interregional connections before local transmission occurred.

  outbreak in a specific area was influenced by population size,
  urbanization, and elevation, but not by temperature or humidity.

  provided support for models that emphasize the importance of
  local and long-distance interactions in the spread of the virus.

to use adaptive dose finding methods, which allow the experiment to adjust the dose levels based on interim data to better target the most effective dose.  Historically, such adaptive processes were found to be suspicious by the FDA, leading to concerns that they could be used to manipulate test results and obscure safety issues.  These doubts were addressed by proving that under reasonable conditions, the adaptive dose finding rule doesn't affect the distribution of the p-value in relation to the true hazard ratio.  Additionally, we investigated the impact of using an incorrect prior distribution on data, discovering that even when the prior is poorly chosen, it won't affect overall false positive error rates, although it can increase the false negative error rate if the chosen dose is suboptimal.  We also examined the properties of several well-known dose finding methods using simulated data and real clinical trial data sets.  Our research provides the theoretical foundation for supporting the use of Bayesian adaptive dose finding methods in clinical trials.  The results of our study are applicable to clinical trials involving two stages, including those with Phase 1/2 design, and involve continuous or binary endpoint measurements.  The methods we studied are primarily geared towards minimizing toxic events while maximizing the treatment's therapeutic effects, and can be characterized as being Bayesian, adaptive, and efficiency-driven.  The data we used was collected over a 20-year period, spanning from 1999 to 2018, and was obtained from clinical trial databases, including ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed.  The standard we used to evaluate the methods' performance is based on conducting further investigations, and involves checking the equality of the observed hazard ratios' distributions with respect to the assumed gamma distribution, and verifying that the estimated optimal dose corresponds to the true one, and that the p-value's distribution remains unchanged in relation to the actual hazard ratio.  The methods we studied employ reversible jump posterior sampling, and include Bayesian adaptive dose finding methods such as SPRT-based, NPLI-based, and isotonic regression-based techniques, including the recently introduced efficient and Bayesian (eB) method, and the cumulative hazard-based isotonic regression (CHIR) method.  The data we used was preprocessed to extract relevant information, including calculating p-values, estimating optimal doses, conducting further investigations, and analyzing endpoint measurements.  The outcomes of our studies are applicable to clinical trials involving binary or continuous endpoint measurements, including those with Phase 1/2 design, and provide the theoretical foundation for supporting the use of Bayesian adaptive dose finding methods in clinical trials. Lymph nodes contain diverse populations of immune cells, including
dendritic cells that play a crucial role in recognizing pathogens and
modulating the immune response.
This research employed serial EM to reconstruct lymph nodes from mice
infected with the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, allowing for the detailed
analysis of dendritic cells within these nodes.
The reconstructions revealed that dendritic cells primarily occupy the
lymph node's medullary cavity and have distinct, intermingled populations
in the cortical and medullary sinuses.
The study found that Toxoplasma infection causes an increase in the number
of dendritic cells in the lymph nodes and a shift in their distribution,
with more cells found in the medullary cavity where it is thought they
interact with macrophages that contain the parasite.
The high-resolution images also enabled the visualization of the
extracellular matrix that surrounds the lymph node's dendritic cells and
sinus-residing cells, providing new insights into its composition and
organization.
Furthermore, the reconstructions facilitated the creation of a detailed
model of the lymph node's medullary cavity and its surrounding walls,
allowing for calculations of specific cellular component volumes and
providing evidence for the presence of a particular dendritic cell shape
that was previously described in two-dimensional EM images. 
The comprehensive data from this study have been made publicly available
through the Center for Big Data in the Life Sciences.

We have adapted this problem to three-dimensional space and are referring to it as the 6D pose estimation geometric problem. 

  In its basic form, the planar Euclidean distance geometric problem can be solved using a direct method. However, the 6D pose estimation geometric problem lacks a comparable efficient solution approach. To address this issue, we have developed an indirect method for solving the 6D pose estimation geometric problem. 

  In specific cases, the planar Euclidean distance geometric problem can be solved using an over-determined system of nonlinear equations. This is achievable when all input points lie on a flat plane. When this condition is not met, we have found that using an over-determined system yields a less accurate outcome. 

  In contrast to existing research, our indirect method first projects the 3D space onto the yz-plane and then constructs an over-determined system of nonlinear equations to find the map. This approach provides a more precise solution compared to existing methods and is supported by our experimental data. 

  We have tested our indirect method on a dataset that includes multiple types of non-planar configurations and observed a notable improvement in outcome accuracy. 

  The code for our indirect method has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/linhson0507/PoseEstimation.

As the channel's aspect ratio decreases, the transport transition from ballistic to diffuse behavior can take an unexpected detour through a regime we've identified as a snaking pattern of stable islands. These islands arise due to a complex interplay between the curvature of the transport regime's boundary and the non-uniform distribution of scattering on the channel's walls. As a result, the transition through the snaking pattern can become asymmetric, depending on the direction of movement. The channels' geometry that exhibit a snaking pattern of stable islands can be realized in a waveguide with a microcavity, using a beam splitter as the source of uneven boundary scattering. As such systems are commonly used in quantum computing, understanding the snaking pattern of stable islands can be crucial for ensuring reliable operation. In conclusion, the snaking pattern of stable islands provides a theoretical framework for understanding particle transport in a channel with uneven boundary scattering, and can be applied to a variety of systems, including a waveguide with a microcavity, through the inclusion of scattering induced by a photonic cavity, resulting in an altered transport behavior. To address this interdependence, we develop a methodology for applying compositional verification techniques to ensure the correctness of complex systems featuring multiple process components. uncertainty in climate change predictions stems
  from high-latitude seasonal ice, specifically the Beaufort Sea. Studies
  with varying levels of complexity have investigated this issue but agree
  that the feedback loop between temperature, ice cover, and atmospheric
  conditions is crucial. A key phenomenon affecting this loop is the
  appearance of warm water beneath the ice. To better understand and model
  this behavior, we drew from existing research on the same topic but with
  a focus on the Baltic Sea. There, a similar phenomenon is driven by
  changes in wind patterns. To capture the effect of warm water on ice and
  atmosphere, we propose a new term in the energy balance equation, based
  on the temperature difference between the ocean and ice surface. This
  term, in turn, is influenced by the amount of warm water beneath the
  ice. To determine this value, we developed a simple model of ocean
  temperature, relying on inputs of atmospheric and oceanic currents.
  This model, in turn, is informed by data on ocean and atmospheric
  currents in the Arctic. To account for the impact of warm water on
  atmospheric feedback, we drew from research on the same topic but with
  a focus on the Baltic Sea. There, changes in water temperature were
  found to affect atmospheric circulation patterns. To evaluate the
  significance of warm water on ice and atmosphere, we conducted a
  sensitivity analysis with our combined ice-ocean-atmosphere model.
  This analysis revealed that reducing the effect of warm water on
  atmospheric circulation from very strong to strong resulted in a
  shift from positive to negative hysteresis in the Beaufort Sea region,
  indicating a threshold for feedback loop behavior. Below this
  threshold, increasing summer sea ice cover leads to increased winter
  cover, while above it, the relationship is reversed. A second
  sensitivity analysis showed that this loop can be influenced by
  changes in atmospheric circulation patterns, specifically the
  appearance of high-pressure systems over the ocean. These
  circulation patterns raise the temperature of the ocean surface,
  accelerating ice cover loss, and thus exacerbating the loop
  feedback. However, this loop can be stabilized by increased
  winter ice cover, as it results in expanded sea ice, and thus
  reduced ocean surface temperature. As a result, we conclude that
  warm water beneath the ice plays a crucial role in the hysteresis
  loop

  feedback from massive stars disrupts the formation of gas clouds by heating
  them through UV radiation and high-energy particles.  We've modified the
  ARENA code to incorporate this type of feedback and modeled 7 massive star
  forming regions using a 25 parsec^3 sub-region of the galaxy evolution
  simulation.  By modeling the effects of radiative feedback on surrounding
  clouds, we found it prevents the formation of dense, star-forming clouds in
  areas already experiencing high levels of star formation.  However, it
  facilitates the formation of dense clouds in more remote areas, thus
  potentially explaining the observed pattern of dense cloud distribution
  patterns in galaxies.  This effect is short-lived, as the same clouds may
  be driven away from those areas by supernova feedback.  This impact is
  particularly noticeable in low-mass galaxy hierarchies, where the range
  of cloud distribution is more narrowly confined, in contrast to high-mass
  galaxy hierarchies, where a wider variety of cloud distributions are
  observed.  This feedback also leads to the creation of large, low-density
  clouds that may eventually coalesce into more massive clouds, thus fuel
  ing the formation of the most massive stars.  This process is slowed in
  galaxies with vigorous star formation as more clouds are pushed to the
  edges of the simulation domain, where they are torn apart by tidal
  forces.  This analysis provides a foundation for understanding the role
  of radiative feedback in galaxy hierarchies and suggests that it plays
  a key role in the formation of massive star forming clouds.  This is
  supported by observations of the famous star forming region W3, which
  is composed of a large, low-density cloud with a dense, star forming
  core at its center.  This feedback also influences the formation of
  gas clouds on remote areas by driving them to form more remotely in a
  process that's fueled by the energy released from massive stars, thus
  potentially explaining the observed correlation between star formation
  activity and remote gas cloud distribution patterns observed in
  galaxies.  This analysis can be applied to individual star forming
  regions, while a broader perspective is necessary to understand its
  impact on the surrounding environment.  This is necessary to accurately
  model the formation of gas clouds and their subsequent collapse into

  in the study of transport properties in disordered materials, particularly 
  graphite and carbon-based systems. However, the precise definition of the 
  tube diameter requires resolution, as it is indirectly measured through 
  transport properties that are influenced by both disorder and curvature 
  effects within the tubes. This ambiguity hinders a thorough understanding 
  of the model's underlying physics. Recent research reveals that the tube 
  diameter can be determined directly from measurements of the Hall 
  conductivity, leading to the discovery that individual graphene layer 
  curvature generates significant tube diameters (>1 nm) and varied 
  distribution patterns, depending on the source of curvature (point 
  defects, grain boundaries, and surface roughness). This finding challenges 
  previous assumptions about the minimum disorder required to activate 
  transport within the tube model, allowing for the prediction of 
  conductivity activation levels based solely on curvature measurements. 
  Consequently, curvature analysis is shown to be a more precise and 
  non-destructive method for determining the tube model parameters, 
  offering significant implications for the understanding and manipulation 
  of transport properties in graphene and related materials. 
  The approach outlined in the study can be applied to other systems, 
  such as phosphorene, where curvature also controls tube diameters and 
  influences transport activation levels, and can be modified to assess 
  tube model parameters in relation to curvature in 4-layer graphene, 
  few-layer graphite, and van der Waals materials under pressure. 
  This research demonstrates that curvatures both small and large are 
  crucial for understanding transport and conductivity in disordered 
  carbon-based systems. 
  The findings related to graphene and phosphorene are validated through 
  simultaneous measurements of conductivity and curvature using 
  scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy under operating conditions, 
  facilitating real-time, non-destructive analysis of disorder and 
  curvature effects on transport and conductivity in individual layers 
  of material, allowing for the assessment of tube model parameters 
  and predicting conductivity activation levels based on curvature 
  measurements alone. 
  The discovery that curvature spontaneously activates transport within 
  the tube model has far-reaching implications for enhancing and controllable 
  transport in graphene and related materials, providing a rationale 
  for revising growth and deposition methods to exploit naturally 
  occurring curvature for device application, and revealing that 
  small (>=1 nm) curvature yields tube diameters that activate 
  transport at lower disorder

on Differential and Integral Equations, presenting a review of recent developments in the study of time-one map properties for non-autonomous dynamical systems described by parabolic equations. A specific correlation is drawn between the classical work of Laslett and the current research landscape, highlighting key findings and generalizing them to non-autonomous systems. Some important theorems and our original theorem providing sufficient conditions for the time-one map to be smooth are also offered as contributions to the issue. 

Our original theorem extends a theorem by Zhong and Chen, being applicable to a broader class of systems and offering an alternative approach to establishing the smoothness of time-one maps. This, in turn allows us to discuss the local smoothness of solutions to parabolic equations and the non-uniqueness of solutions to certain integral equations. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these results and the classical work of Laslett, revealing that his findings can be obtained using our theorem. 

In the concluding section, we outline potential future research directions related to time-one map properties and the local smoothness of solutions to parabolic equations. 

The paper is addressed to a broad audience with an interest in differential and integral equations, offering an interdisciplinary blend of mathematics, physics, and engineering applications. 

The research reported in the paper was conducted at the Institute of Mathematics at Nanjing University under the guidance of Professor Xiangx1 Wang, renowned for his expertise in partial differential equations and parabolic equations, in particular. 

The paper is written by Zhongyong, a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Mathematics at Nanjing University, in collaboration with Xiangx1 Wang, his supervisor, and Jin Lee, a distinguished visiting scholar also from the same institution. 

The paper is divided into six sections, introducing the context and background information, presenting our original theorem, discussing its implications for the local smoothness of solutions to parabolic equations, exploring the connection with the classical work of Laslett, and outlining potential future research directions. 

The paper utilizes a variety of mathematical notation, presenting derivations using classical calculus, operational calculus, and semigroup theory, and incorporating the classical work of Laslett, the fundamental work of Feller, the operational calculus developed by Daletskii and Mel'nikov, the theory of parabolic equations developed by PDE experts Chen, Zhong, and Wang, the semigroup theory developed by PDE expert Goldstein, and the research on time-one map properties conducted by PDE experts Zhong, Chen, and Wang.

A twin group of a planar graph can be formed by creating multiple copies of the same graph, some of which are connected by blue edges, and then removing the red edges from the connections between these copies.  The remaining blue edges in this constructed graph are then given a 2-edge coloring.  The key property of a twin group is that its 2-edge coloring can be determined by the arrangement of the original planar graph.  The concept of a virtual twin group can be thought of as a generalization of a twin group where the blue edges are represented as dashed lines instead of actual edges.   and memory requirements, making it an highly effective solution for large-scale 
  tensor data processing. We have open-sourced TANSEN, inviting further research 
  collaborations and advancements in the field.

  is a compressed and simplified version of the parent model. This compression 
  is achieved through a novel weight pruning method called TANSEN-weight pruning, 
  which is specifically tailored to tensors. In contrast to existing weight pruning 
  techniques, TANSEN-weight pruning uses tensor capabilities to enhance the method 
  itself, resulting in a significant model compression of up to  99.9% in terms

  channels by compressing speech signals. In 1993, the ITU-P.80 standard was
  established to cater to various low-bit-rate speech coding applications.
  However, with the advent of new technologies and expanding communication
  bandwidth, the ITU-P.80 standard's limitations became apparent, particularly
  in its inability to manage multiple, simultaneous conversations and poor
  performance in noisy environments. Consequently, the ITU G.729.8 codec was
  developed as a side-channel speech coder to enhance the ITU-P.80 standard.
  The ITU G.729.8 codec operates at two bandwidths, 5.8 and 6.4 kbps, and
  is designed to improve the ITU-P.80 standard's speech quality in various
  scenarios by accepting auxiliary information about the speech signal.
  Auxiliarily-fed speech coders, like the ITU G.729.8 codec, can be used in
  various applications, including wireless communications, multi-party
  conversations, and listening environments with significant background noise.
  Research on auxiliarily-fed coders focuses on improving the performance of
  existing speech codes by feeding them with side information, and relatively
  few studies have explored the development of such coders from scratch.
  Therefore, in this work, a new auxiliarily-fed speech coder, called the
  Slant-Shaped Code (SSC), was proposed and tested to evaluate its
  performance. The SSC codec operates at a bandwidth of 6.4 kbps and is
  suitable for wireless communications, multi-party conversations, and listening
  environments with significant background noise.
  The proposed SSC codec consists of three stages: the Slant-Shaped Encoder
  (SSE), the Memory-Based Quantizer (MBQ), and the Post-Processing Module
  (PPM). The SSE stage compresses the speech signal using a slant-shaped
  distribution model, the MBQ stage employs a memory-based quantizer to
  compress the encoded speech, and the PPM stage uses a post-processing
  module to refine the coded speech.
  To train the SSC codec, a large dataset of 8,000 clean speech files was
  compiled, along with three smaller datasets containing background noise
  corresponding to different SNR levels. The codec was evaluated on the TID
  database, which includes six different speech coders, and on the proposed
  smaller datasets.

We have investigated the statistics of a key measure of a system's complexity - the angle between its eigenvectors and those of its uncoupled version - in both theoretical models and a real-world application using atmospheric data from a reanalysis.  These studies showed that the distribution of these angles is non-uniform and can be described by a specific probability distribution, which we call the "Dirac-Delta Double-Weibull" distribution.  We found that the statistics of this distribution vary significantly depending on the frequency of a particular geophysical oscillation.  Specifically, the distribution's shape factors are directly correlated with the oscillation's frequency and its own statistical distribution.  In the context of atmospheric data, this means that the distribution of the angles is non-uniform and changes over periods of weeks to months, reflecting variations in the speed of global circulation patterns.  However, when considering the combined effects of different frequency ranges, the statistics of the distribution of the angles become more uniform and no longer reflect the specifics of the distribution of the parent oscillation.  We believe that the Dirac-Delta Double-Weibull distribution provides a useful tool for analyzing the statistics of a system's complexity and could have implications for understanding the effects of the forcing of a system on its own complexity.  As such, it may be a useful component in developing more accurate predictions of future states of the climate system. involves understanding how effectively neural networks can withstand intentionally crafted input data errors. To address this issue, researchers frequently employ robust training methods to enhance performance. Nevertheless, our research indicates that neural networks can successfully recognize and differentiate minor, commonplace image distortions, such as rotation and scaling, even without robust training. In fact, our findings reveal that these neural networks preferentially misclassify such subtle distortions more often when classifying between similar object categories than when distinguishing between more distinct objects. Consequently, our analysis suggests that, in certain situations, seemingly adverse data fluctuations may actually amount to diverse, novel data that neural networks can process easily. To demonstrate this concept of "diverse data" more clearly, we developed a novel, high-precision method for identifying pixels associated with these minor distortions across an image. This allows for the creation of synthetic, high-fidelity diverse data that can be used for various machine learning applications, such as model fine-tuning and data augmentation. Our approach also enables the calculation of specific distortion effects on various object categories and the calculation of frequent, composite patterns of these minor distortions. Overall, our research highlights the positive aspects of minor image distortions and explores innovative ways to work with them. To facilitate further research in this area, we are making our diverse data generator publicly available. Airborne Spectropolarimeter, a remote-sensing instrument designed to measure the polarization patterns and spectral properties of light in various parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, covering wavelengths from visible to short-wave infrared ranges. The airborne spectropolarimeter features a horizontal scan pattern and includes three polarization filters to detect different polarization orientations. By processing the data, the instrument can provide fully resolved polarization and spectral profiles for numerous ground targets. We demonstrate the capabilities of the Beijing Airborne Spectropolarimeter through flight tests conducted above the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in China and the Kangerluisa Sermmeraqa Fjord in Greenland. These experiments showed the instrument's effectiveness in collecting high-quality data across diverse environments and highlight its potential for improving the analysis of remotely sensed data by incorporating polarization information. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of the instrument to enhance the identification of polarimetric targets by analyzing the retrieved spectra and polarization patterns in data obtained from flight tests conducted above the Gobi Desert in China and the Antarctic Plateau in China. These results indicate that the instrument can easily adapt to a wide range of operating heights and environments, making it suitable for widespread application. However, to fully realize the instrument's capabilities, we emphasize the necessity of developing comprehensive libraries of polarimetric targets based on field measurements conducted across various ecosystems. By doing so, the instrument and associated analysis can be optimized to provide accurate results even in situations where targets are partially covered by water, snow, or sand. Additionally, we highlight the need for a deeper understanding of the relationships between polarimetric properties, radiation interference, cloud cover, and atmospheric conditions to minimize data loss during analysis. Lastly, we outline the future development pathways for the instrument, suggesting upgrades that could expand its operational height, enhance data processing algorithms, and expand its spectral range to better utilize the potential of remotely sensed data. By realizing these developments, the instrument can be further leveraged to address complex environmental issues in regions like the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the Gobi Desert, and the Antarctic Plateau. The code and data for this study are available at: 10.6083/19Tg1023.6110. The instrument and associated research have significant implications for the analysis of remotely sensed data in various fields and can be applied to study the polarimetric properties of targets in diverse ecosystems across the visible to short-wave infrared ranges. Therefore, we believe that the development of the Beijing Airborne Spectropolarimeter and associated algorithms serves as an invaluable template for constructing similar instruments

Each skill can be thought of as a separate neural function that can be trained and utilized independently. For example, the ability to recognize objects is like a visual skill, whereas hearing someone speak is a different auditory skill. What's unique about neural networks is the way they can blend these individual skills together through reconfiguration, much like how humans combine different sensory inputs to process new information. To better understand and address this issue, a retrospective analysis was conducted of medical records at a large Swedish hospital that primarily administered the AstraZeneca vaccine.  The study covered a six-week period during the pandemic's peak and included 13,908 individuals who received the AstraZeneca vaccine without a prior history of blood clotting disorders.  The researchers identified 42 cases of blood clots in the brains and other key blood vessels that required immediate medical attention.  The estimated incidence of these conditions was 4.77 cases per 1,000 vaccinated individuals.  The typical Swedish age-related incidence of these conditions was used for comparison and revealed a 52-fold increased risk among those who received the AstraZeneca vaccine.  However, the overall mortality rate associated with the vaccine was 6 percent, which was comparable to the expected mortality rate without treatment.  The study's findings also suggested that blood clots in the lungs and other areas occurred at a similar frequency as brain blood clots.  The age and sex of the individuals, as well as underlying medical conditions, did not affect the risk of blood clots.  Notably, the study discovered a 11 to 16 day median duration between the inoculation and the onset of blood clot symptoms.  The researchers concluded that while the AstraZeneca vaccine may increase the risk of blood clots in rare instances, the majority of those affected survive with treatment, and the vaccine's overall mortality benefit likely outweighs its side effects, especially among older adults at high risk of severe COVID-19 symptoms.  The study's results may help inform vaccination strategies and the management of potential blood clot complications in individuals who receive the AstraZeneca vaccine.  Due to the vaccine's temporary suspension in several countries, the study's findings may have implications for its eventual reinstatement.  The researchers suggest monitoring for blood clots in the 11 to 16 day post-inoculation window and exploring the use of alternative vaccines for individuals at high risk of blood clots.  The study's results also highlight the importance of reporting adverse reactions to blood clots in the post-inoculation period.  The authors propose further research into the underlying causes of blood clots in vaccine recipients, potentially through comparisons with individuals who experienced blood clots without receiving the vaccine, and investigating the presence of specific immune system proteins associated with blood clots in vaccine

Within the EOM framework, we examine the change in measurable differences over time and derive an important inequality relating the quantum mechanical trace distance to a particular dissipation factor. Notably, this inequality's structure is analogous to a well-known inequality in classical ergodic theory, thereby enabling us to apply an ergodic theorem to obtain a quantum mechanics counterpart. This quantum mechanics counterpart demonstrates that under certain conditions, the time-evolved initial mixed state will display a form of universality, effectively blurring the distinction between different initial states as time progresses. We further analyze the scope and limitations of this findings, considering both the EOM and other similar models, including the Jaynes-Cummings model, in order to gain a deeper understanding of this universality phenomenon. We conclude our discussion by exploring the implications of this findings for the ergodic quantum mechanics and its underlying assumptions, highlighting the critical role of continuous measurements. We stress that this measurements-driven ergodicity is driven by a distinct mechanism than the one observed in closed quantum systems, offering a potential explanation for the prevalence of this universality among open quantum systems. We propose that future research should prioritize exploring measurement-driven ergodicity beyond the realm of thermalization. We also emphasize that in contrast to the classical ergodic theory, measurement-driven ergodicity in quantum mechanics is characterized by a pervasively emergent randomness rather than a universally emerging set, thereby requiring a major revision of our understanding of this phenomenon. We further note that this research direction is connected to the infamous quantum scrambling phenomenon, suggesting that both share a common underlying mechanism. We propose that future research should prioritize exploring the measurements-driven ergodicity in quantum systems, focusing on both theoretical and experimental approaches, and considering various models, including chaotic and complex systems, to gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon. We also emphasize that measuring ergodicity in quantum systems is significantly more intricate than measuring scrambling, due to the sensitivity of ergodicity indicators to noise and errors in measurements. We propose that developing robust and precise indicators of ergodicity in quantum systems will necessitate a major breakthrough in quantum measurement technology, capable of detecting the emergent randomness across multiple degrees of freedom in both global and local measurements. We further note that achieving this level of precision will likely necessitate utilizing more sophisticated quantitative methodologies to measure ergodicity, such as tracing the growth of trace distance or the emergence of entanglement entropy,

This approach yields an alternative characterization of Gaussian measures, which deviates from the conventional characterization based on characteristic function analysis. In particular, we've established that a measure $\gamma$ is Gaussian if and only if there exists a unique minimum to the functional $I_\gamma (C)\cdot \gamma e^1$, where $I_\gamma$ represents the Wasserstein-2 distance between measures and $e^1$ denotes the Dirac measure. electromagnetic interactions that affect the distribution of excitons.

option for the use in quantum memories.  This hypothesis is tested
by simulating a controlled phase flip of a exciton and detecting the
result after varying amounts of time.

In this research, we developed a new algorithm to solve systems of polynomial equations in the context of positive real arrangement, a specialized case that includes polynomials with non-negative coefficients.  Specifically, we considered the ring of positive semi-definite polynomials, a recent theoretical advancement.  Our algorithm, dubbed the 'descending flow method,' leverages the positive real arrangement and the properties of the ring to solve systems of polynomial equations.  We demonstrated the applicability and efficiency of the descending flow method to various problems, including unconditional positivity criteria for polynomials, the solvability of systems of polynomial equations in the positive real numbers, and the characterization of totally positive functions.  Our method offers an alternative to other approaches like Groebner basis, real algebraic geometry, and the use of relaxation linear programming, providing a more efficient solution for systems of polynomial equations with non-negative coefficients.  Furthermore, the descending flow method enables the determination of the exact number of non-negative roots of a single polynomial equation or a system of polynomial equations.  We evaluated the descending flow method's performance on numerous examples, including conditions for positivity of various functions, both classic and recent, showcasing the method's versatility.   demonstrates that VPGG's flexible nature allows it to be tailored to

  variable-precision drawing method. As a result, VPGG achieves significant
  improvements in terms of sketch size, query performance, and overall
  efficiency. To further illustrate the versatility of VPGG, the paper

We developed a dynamic model of a developing economy with an evolving skill distribution and used it to analyze the effects of state capacity on income inequality. State capacity can take various forms, such as a strong military or a well-functioned bureaucracy, and we represented this capability as a parameter that affects how resources are allocated to education, agriculture, or industry. Our findings indicate that state capacity initially leads to greater income inequality as more unequal distribution of education benefits results in greater disparities in skills and income. Our model suggests that state capacity influenced income inequality as it evolved over time, with stronger states leading to more equal societies, especially during times of significant economic change. traffic lights is a complex problem that
  has been difficult to solve with the increasing demand for autonomous vehicles.
  Utilizing RGB images from a vehicle in motion provides the primary data for
  this estimation, making it challenging due to the partial and obscured views
  of traffic lights. This issue is further complicated by the need for real-time
  processing to accommodate potential uses in autonomous vehicle navigation.
  The proposed framework, called FusedDeep, addresses these difficulties by
  incorporating a novel method that fuses features from different stages of a
  convolutional neural network to enhance the description of traffic lights.
  Initially, the network extracts coarse global features through a standard CNN
  architecture, and then a complementary module, designed to capture additional
  local features, fuses them with the global features using a novel fusion
  mechanism. The fused features are then used to generate high-accuracy binary
  masks of traffic lights. The model is trained end-to-end to predict the 3D
  coordinates of traffic lights using a small set of 3D annotations without
  LiDAR. The evaluation of FusedDeep on five cities using real-world driving
  images shows a significant improvement in estimating traffic light locations
  compared to existing baselines, demonstrating its potential in facilitating
  autonomous vehicle navigation. The proposed framework demonstrates the
  capability of feature fusion to enhance the description of traffic lights and
  accurately estimate their 3D locations even in partially obscured views. The

The topic of curated attributed event sequences has gained interest lately, with researchers developing methods to generalize to novel, unstructured events.  In contrast, the uncurited version remains underexplored, representing a more challenging scenario where events lack a clear beginning or end and new attributes emerge continuously.  The best approach to handle this scenario remains unknown.  In response to this challenge, we introduce a new framework called AEDISC, combining attributed event detection with structured learning to accommodate complex, uncurited patterns.  The design leverages attributed events as guidance to derive meaningful, structured representations from raw input data.  Through rigorous evaluation, AEDISC demonstrates its superiority over alternative methods in three domains:  virtual agents, customer service conversations, and open-ended written interactions.  The approach shows particular benefits in attributing events accurately and generating coherent, structured outputs in response to input events.  In addition to positive results, future research directions are also identified.  The code and models for AEDISC are available at https://github.com/ghuifeng/AEDISC.  With the success of AEDISC, it is proposed that future work on attributed event sequences prioritize a parallel track focusing on structured outputs.  This track is exemplified by implementing AEDISC on a specific dataset, resulting in a model that generates structured output corresponding to complex, uncurited patterns in text.  In contrast to current approaches that treat input and output as separate entities, this new track treats the input and output as interconnected, refining the approach by introducing a novel structured learning objective that can adapt to changing event patterns.  The approach is enabled by a new discourse-aware memory network, eliminating the need for explicit event boundaries. Higman proved under the assumption of the axiom of choice: for any set of finite strings made up of symbols from some infinite set, there's an infinite sequence of numbers where each number corresponds to a unique string from the given set, and the associated sequence of strings forms a well-ordered chain under the relation defined by first occurrence.  This more specific version of Higman's Lemma can be used to demonstrate the existence of certain infinite sequences of finite strings made up of characters from the real numbers, which are also well-ordered under the relation defined by first occurrence.  These specific sequences of strings are analogous to, but more general than, the nested sequences of digits commonly found in mathematical representations of the irrational numbers e and pi.  Each of these sequences generates a unique real number, often referred to as an "algebraic continued fraction" or "regular fraction", which corresponds to the original set of nested parentheses that define it.  These real numbers, when considered as a single, unified entity, share properties such as being transcendental, having specific arithmetic characteristics like being normal, and occupying unique positions within specific sets of real numbers, often characterized by congruence relations.  The method of proof for Higman's Lemma allows for the stronger conclusion that for any given finite height, there's a corresponding sequence of characters and a height of that particular sequence, all of which require the application of only a finite amount of choice.   least expensive generating unit. 
  This approach provides an equitable solution, as each generator is paid a 
  capacity fee equal to its marginal cost, ensuring they are willing to 
  provide capacity when needed.

  linear optimization models, eliminating the need for separate adequacy 
  assessments. 
  It is essential to note that this approach does not account for uncertainty 
  and relies on forward contracts to manage future demand.

This approach involves expressing the system's thermodynamic functions in terms of its equilibrium properties under various driving forces and particle densities. This problem is a variation of the prime oracle problem, which is a well-studied topic in computational number theory. When the oracle is set to the first prime number, we can simply use it to determine if a number is prime, but for a fixed non-palindromic positive integer N, we show that there is a prime-oracle Turing machine that decides whether N is prime or not with a step complexity of O(p_n), where p_n represents the n-th prime number. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of at least p_n +5 steps for solving this problem with a prime-oracle Turing machine for a fixed non-palindromic positive integer N. When the oracle is set to the r-th prime number, we demonstrate that there are pairs of prime numbers, both greater than a r, that differ by r, which contributes to the complexity of determining whether N is prime or not. As the number of edge devices continues to escalate, leveraging the substantial amounts of data generated by the public is becoming increasingly vital to accelerate ML model development.  Although open and licensed data can be used for model training, securing permission to use private and paid data from devices poses significant challenges.  This work introduces FedVis, a novel framework designed to facilitate secure, private, and paid data sharing from edge devices with limited resources, in return for incentives.  FedVis employs a cutting-edge technique called Neural Network-based Reasoning to streamline interactions with devices, enabling them to provide logical justifications for data sharing based on personalized considerations.  As a proof-of-concept, FedVis was applied to a real-world example involving a mobile app, demonstrating its capability to recruit willing participants from the public, secure private data from them, and combine this with open and licensed data for secure, private, and parallel model training.   This paper presents GraphAR, a conflict resolution framework designed
  for large-scale RDF and property graph databases, capable of handling
  complex conflicts of deletion, insertion, and modification types.
  GraphAR leverages an advanced, highly efficient arbitration method
  to resolve conflicts at both the data and property levels, employing
  user-defined functions and predicates to address system ambiguities.
  This framework enables customization through user-provided functions
  and predicates, allowing users to incorporate domain-specific logic
  and prioritize data integrity, security, and performance metrics.
  GraphAR supports transactional updates, provides atomic operations
  to ensure data consistency, and includes a query rewrite mechanism
  to ensure compatibility with the uncertain nature of partially resolved
  conflicts, thereby enabling effective query processing.
  This framework includes an evaluation of various arbitration strategies
  and a performance analysis under scaling conditions, in addition to
  comparing GraphAR with existing solutions using benchmarks and real-world
  datasets, showcasing its capabilities and efficiency in practice.

  being integrated into existing systems and executed on prominent cloud platforms.

  research in conflict resolution for large-scale RDF and property graph
  databases, and provides a solid foundation for developing and testing
  various arbitration strategies, as well as exploring innovative conflict
  resolution techniques in graph-based systems.

  limitations and their own generation processes.  This knowledge can then be 
  utilised to improve the systems by teaching them what distinguishes natural 
  human conversations from artificial ones.  We tested this approach on two 
  dialogue datasets and discovered that it yields superior results when evaluating 
  the systems' ability to differentiate between human-like and artificial 
  conversations.  As a consequence, our proposed method can be employed to 
  develop more natural and human-like dialogue systems by incorporating the 
  knowledge about artificial generation marks that characterise such systems.

Current cross-view classification models are largely based on supervised learning and suffer from several issues:  they require extensive labeled data, have poor generalization abilities, and are expensive to develop.  In contrast, we propose a novel, semi-supervised framework called Cross-View Class Invariance (CVCI), which leverages the uniqueness of the universal invariant class across views without using labeled data.  The CVCI model is based on VAEs and incorporates an encoder and decoder that map images across views as invariant classes, thereby facilitating class-based data sharing and transfer learning without additional annotations.  Experimental evaluations on five diverse datasets demonstrate the superiority of CVCI in comparison to state-of-the-art models in both natural and man-made object classification scenarios.  Code and datasets are available at \url{https://github.com/ShiQiangViBAC/CVCI}.  The understanding of the universal invariant class's role in the absence of labeled data paves the way for the exploration of other inherent properties that can be exploited for model development.  Future research can be directed towards the study of additional inherent properties and the design of more robust, generalizable models using only a few labeled examples. RNNs can access past inputs directly, but future input information is essential for effective performance, and must be carefully integrated using memory augmentation strategies.  Unfortunately, existing literature lacks a unifying framework to explain how these methods augment memory.  Without a clear understanding of their workings, optimizing RNNs is a difficult task.  In this research, we developed a theoretical framework to analyze memory augmentation techniques.  Using this framework, we discovered that methods like feedback connections, residual connections, and recurrent skip connections can be characterized as linear, nonlinear, and weighted combinations of past and present information, respectively. Our approach can be employed to interpret and analyze other memory augmentation methods, and can be scaled to more complex networks. As a result, the demand for secure, reliable, and high-speed wireless communication systems has never been greater.  To meet this demand, the Federal Communications Commission plans to conduct large-scale wireless communication spectrum auctions in the near future.  However, the effectiveness of various security methods is likely to be impacted by the choice of wireless communication standard.  In order to fully leverage the potential of the Federal Communications Commission's newly available spectrum, it's essential to choose a wireless standard that securely supports high-speed data transmission.  This research investigates the deep packet inspection resistance and robustness of WPA2-enabled IEEE 802.11ac devices and reveals that they can securely maintain high-speed wireless connections of up to 433.3 Mbps.  Consequently, devices meeting this standard can be used to securely conduct large-scale wireless communication spectrum auctions.  From a practical perspective, this research provides valuable insights for buyers on how to securely purchase used devices and ensures the secure, high-speed data transmission capabilities of WPA2-enabled IEEE 802.11ac devices.  From a theoretical standpoint, this research expands on prior work related to the performance evaluation of WPA2-enabled IEEE 802.11ac devices in terms of throughput, robustness, and deep packet inspection resistance.  In order to facilitate further research and to demonstrate the applicability of this standard for secure, high-speed wireless communications, this research is also being shared publicly as an OpenAirInterface implementation.  Finally, this research paves the way for further exploration of the security of future wireless communication standards such as IEEE 802.11ax and Wi-Fi 6.  In particular, section 6 of this paper highlights potential future research directions related to the deep packet inspection resistance and energy efficiency of Wi-Fi 6 devices that support multiple user connections.  In addition to generating a theoretical framework for secure, high-speed wireless communications, this research also contributes a publicly accessible, bi-directionally configurable OpenAirInterface implementation of WPA2-enabled IEEE 802.11ac devices that meets the performance, robustness and deep packet inspection resistance standards and can securely maintain high-speed wireless connections of up to 433.3 Mbps. Our findings build upon and extend previous research by Berman, Kiefer and Wolf, Knight, and Whitt, and our goal is to provide a unified and accessible account of the asymptotic behavior of the ratio of the supremum to the expectation of the maximum of L\'evy processes. For the specific set of natural numbers defined as $C_n = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\}$, the function $f(C_n)$ is represented as $\Pi_n$, resulting in the observation that $\Pi_1 = 1$, $\Pi_2 = 2$, $\Pi_3 = 6$, and so on. It is also noted that the sequence $\Pi_n$ grows faster than any polynomial of degree $n$, yet for any given $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a constant $C_\epsilon$ where $\Pi_n > n^C$ holds true for enough large $n$. Establishing the primality of a number as equivalent to determining whether that number is a product of prime numbers, the next claim posits that for any integer $a$, the quantity $a\cdot \Pi_a$ will have prime factorization consisting of prime factors equal to $a$, indicating that $a\cdot \Pi_a$ equals $a$ raised to the power of $f(C_a)$. Concluding this initial discussion, it is also worth noting that $f(C_a)$ represents the number of times the prime factor $a$ is counted in the set $C_a$, which is observed as $a-1$ for $2 \leq a$, implying that $a\cdot \Pi_a$ equals $a$ raised to the power of $a-1$, or $(a)^{a-1}$.  This note formalizes three distinct theorems related to $\Pi_n$, starting with theorem 1, which posits that for any real numbers $p$ and $q$ where $p+q \leq 2$, the inequality $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\Pi_n^p}{\Pi_n^q} = 1$ holds true. The formal definition of a limit at a point is then applied to establish that the limit of $\Pi_n$ as $n$ approaches infinity is equal to 1, indicating that theorem 1 can be alternatively stated as $\Pi_n$ approaches 1

COVID-19 pandemic broke out in 2020, 
  various forms of surveillance and containment measures have become 
  commonplace in public areas. As a result, an increased interest has been 
  observed in conducting accuracy, fairness, and privacy-related assessments 
  of conventional contact tracing methods relying on Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and 
  GPS technology. However, an overemphasis on traditional evaluation 
  metrics such as detection and false positive rates may lead to flawed 
  generalizations. Therefore, it is crucial to consider ethical parameters 
  alongside conventional ones when evaluating novel contact tracing solutions 
  and protocols. Furthermore, researchers and developers should avoid 
  manipulating artificial obstacles and adversaries to manipulate results, 
  instead utilizing techniques like reinforcement learning to test the robust 
  resilience of contact tracing systems.  To address these concerns, this 
  paper proposes a set of open issues related to ethical contact tracing, 
  focusing on fair and privacy-preserving aspects, and presenting a test 
  scenario for a COVID-19 contact tracing system based on Bluetooth 
  technology.  Finally, it is essential to establish standardized, diverse, 
  and ethical evaluation criteria for contact tracing systems to guarantee 
  trustworthy and practical implementations in public areas.

  is a critical problem in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI data 
  acquisition can be viewed as measuring a random linear transformation, 
  where the measurement matrix encapsulates the sampling process and 
  the original signal represents the signal that would have been measured 
  if data were collected at full resolution. This paper explores the 
  theoretical framework of compressive sensing to determine whether there 
  exists an exact or approximate inverse of the measurement matrix. 
  If such an inverse exists, signal reconstruction can be achieved through 
  a linear deconvolution process. Otherwise, data analysis indicates 
  that signal reconstruction is possible only if the non-uniqueness of 
  the original signal can be tolerated. The theory also highlights the 
  importance of the measurement matrix being full-rank. In practice,

  also inflict significant economic damage. We propose a new, data-driven approach
  to assess the residual transmission risk of a given level of distancing and
  calculate the resulting epidemic outcomes. This approach can be applied to any
  spatial network but is illustrated using a simplified model for a globally
  interconnected population structured by geographic location. We introduce a
  novel, quantifiable concept of "epidemic remaining energy" to predict the
  future transmission dynamics and associated infections resulting from a
  particular level of distancing. We use this framework to investigate the
  optimal level of distancing measures in relation to existing connectivity
  patterns and demonstrate its applicability to real-world scenarios using
  transportation networks and urban configurations. We also explore the
  long-term outcomes of various data-intensive scenarios, including those
  based on actual US state interconnections and European city relationships.
  Our results across diverse settings consistently show that the optimal
  level of distancing is inversely tied to the existing level of population
  connectivity in a given area, providing crucial insight for public
  health policymakers on how to effectively balance virus mitigation with
  community economic recovery. We make our methodology openly available
  through an interactive web platform enabling users to input their own
  data and predict corresponding epidemic outcomes.  We also highlight the
  limitations of our model and the complexity of real-world scenarios,
  suggesting the necessity for further, more refined model developments.  Further research on alternative models is encouraged to supplement our findings.  We provide the code for our methodology on GitHub and encourage readers to explore the interactive web platform at https://covid-distancing-toolbox.org/.  This platform allows users to input their own data, predict corresponding outcomes, and visualize results for various levels of distancing in different settings.  We also offer a compressed zip file containing the sample data used in our numerical examples for reader reference.  This compressed file includes both the code and sample data necessary to reproduce the results presented in our paper figures.  We make a collective effort to advance knowledge in this area through collaborative research, shared data, and openly available methodology.  We invite readers to engage with our findings, contribute to the development of new models, and utilize the provided tools to address similar challenges in their respective fields of study.  We anticipate that the methodology and outcomes derived from our model will be applicable to future virus transmission scenarios, including those involving new pandemic variants, by examining the impact of varying model parameters on epidemic outcomes. To tackle this challenge, we divide the linear term into multiple blocks with varying lengths, employing a non-$\ell_1$-regularized minimization method to estimate each block, and then combine the results using a weighted average. 

  We establish that under non-stationary $\ell_p$-norm conditions, the proposed estimator for the linear parameter vector achieves the optimal rate of convergence, while the nonlinear component estimator retains a near-optimal rate due to an increased $\ell_q$-norm term, where $p$ and $q$ can be specified. 

  We demonstrate through extensive numerical experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets that our method compares favorably to existing alternatives in terms of both sample size requirements and solution stability. 

  The theoretical findings and algorithmic developments lead to a scalable and efficient solver for a type of nonlinear least squares problems with non-separable costs, enabling data-driven discovery of complex relationships in high-dimensional, non-linear settings without prior knowledge of the underlying structure. 

  The proposed method and associated theory also provide a framework for addressing a range of SPARCL-NLSE problems with varying non-linear components, including generalized additive models, where the conditions on data dimensions, degrees of freedom, and hidden component shapes can be specified. 

  The code for the solver, named REGAL, is implemented using Python and R, with access to both versions available on a public repository. 

  The repository includes additional information, such as installation guidelines, data generation scripts, real-world application examples, and guidance on customizing the solver for specific problems. 

  We encourage researchers to utilize and extend REGAL for solving a broad class of regression problems with complex, non-linear structures in high-dimensional data scenarios. 

  A preliminary version of this research was presented at the 2020 International Conference on Machine Learning, under the title "Robust High-Dimensional Additive Models via Non-$\ell_1$ Regularization". 

  The current expanded version includes an expanded literature review, additional numerical experiments, and a detailed case study on data from multiple Gaussian processes. 

  The results on data from multiple Gaussian processes illustrate the applicability of REGAL to capture complex, nonlinear patterns with varying frequencies and amplitudes in time series datasets with thousands of dimensions, derived from realistic simulations of real-world examples, such as genomic data, financial indices, and weather patterns.

Determining the smallest possible length of a Hamiltonian cycle in a given graph is another related concept, sometimes called the cycle diameter. The term hyperhamiltonian diameter was coined to describe the same property for hypergraphs, where a Hamiltonian cycle's length is defined as the minimum number of edges required to traverse a hypergraph while visiting each vertex exactly once and returning to the original vertex. Our investigation focuses on the robustness of topological structures that provide optimal resistance to extensive node losses, in an environment where new connections are highly costly. We developed a theoretical framework to analyze and optimize the robustness of scale-free networks during a state of full connectivity, utilizing a cost function that considers both node addition and deletion costs. Our model allows us to explore the optimal distribution of nodes with varying degrees that minimize the overall cost of network topology changes, both with and without external influences. We demonstrated that in the absence of external factors, the most resilient architecture features a power-law degree distribution, and by applying a linear cost function, we derived the specific parameters of this distribution that maximize robustness. We also investigated the effects of attachment preferences on network robustness and validated our findings empirically. Our model and theoretical insights into the optimal distribution of node degrees also apply to other scale-free networks formed under similar conditions. Notably, our research revealed that adding nodes to maximize node robustness results in a network with a faster growth rate, a larger critical component during massive node losses, and a higher proportion of critical component nodes. Our findings have implications for designing secure and reliable peer-to-peer systems, as well as for understanding the evolution and robustness of natural systems exhibiting similar growth patterns.
